interactions.summary: A student asks why Dante still needs guidance if poets know the way, and Jiang reframes the question by asking what Virgil adds if Dante already has poetic knowledge.

A student says people need an externalized inner voice so they do not confuse the journey with their own pride, and Jiang compares Virgil to a trainer whose job is not new knowledge but sustained focus.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student interpretation and Jiang approval through analogy.

interactions.summary: The class reads Virgil's explanation that envy belongs to goods diminished by sharing, whereas heavenly goods grow with common possession and make love increase.

claims.claim: Jiang resists the premise that Dante's questions prove ignorance; instead he treats guidance as a different function from raw knowledge.
The student answer Jiang accepts says Virgil functions like an embodied inner voice that keeps Dante from collapsing the journey into prideful self-sufficiency.
Jiang's trainer analogy says Virgil does not primarily add new information but keeps Dante focused enough to enact what he already in some sense knows.
The Canto 15 passage defines envy as attachment to earthly goods that diminish when shared, in contrast to heavenly goods that increase with common possession and multiply love.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil becomes a trainer who mostly says one thing: focus.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang's compact model of why spiritual guidance remains necessary even when knowledge is already present.

signature_moments.moment: The guide is an outside body for the inner voice so the self does not worship its own insight.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you need an outside other entity
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It connects poetic guidance directly to anti-pride discipline.

signature_moments.moment: In Heaven, the more people can say 'ours,' the more good and love there is for each.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the more there are who should say ours
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the poem's anti-envy economics in a single memorable formula.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's practical name for what Virgil supplies: disciplined attention more than novel information.
The heavenly form of common possession where sharing enlarges rather than reduces the good held by each.
Goods that provoke envy because dividing them seems to leave less for each possessor.

chronology_notes.note: Here the June 26 discussion welds a pedagogical claim about guides and focus directly onto Dante's envy passage about goods that shrink or grow under sharing.
